name: GHRP-6
maker: None marketed; designed by Cyril Bowers' group (SmithKline code SKF-110679)

overview.headline: The first growth-hormone-releasing peptide, built in a laboratory in the early 1980s and never approved anywhere.
overview.lede: GHRP-6 was designed by Cyril Bowers' group before anyone knew which receptor it worked on; that receptor later turned out to be the one for ghrelin, the hunger hormone. It was studied in the 1990s and 2000s as a GH stimulant and as part of a diagnostic test, then abandoned. Today it exists only as a "research chemical" and a doping agent.

mechanism.intro: A synthetic copy of ghrelin's signal at the receptor that releases GH and drives hunger.

parts.name: Ghrelin receptor (GHS-R1a)
parts.text: Activating it in the pituitary releases a short, dose-related burst of GH within the hour; it works best alongside the body's own GHRH.

parts.name: Appetite
parts.text: The same receptor in the hypothalamus triggers hunger, the effect most often reported with GHRP-6.

parts.name: Cortisol, prolactin, blood sugar
parts.text: GHRPs briefly raise cortisol and prolactin; FDA's safety review also notes possible effects on blood glucose through reduced insulin sensitivity.

more.title: More: a research tool that was never meant to be a drug
paras: GHRP-6 was made as an analogue of the opioid peptide met-enkephalin that had lost its opioid activity but kept a surprising ability to release GH; the hunt for its receptor led to the discovery of ghrelin in 1999. Cuban researchers have studied it for heart and tissue protection, almost entirely in animals.

results.headline: What human studies measured: GH peaks and a diagnostic test. Nothing on body composition.
results.lede: No placebo-controlled trial has tested GHRP-6 for muscle, fat, recovery, healing or ageing in people. The human record is single-dose hormone studies, diagnostic-test validations and one pharmacokinetic study.

stats.lbl: human trials of GHRP-6 as a treatment for any condition
adults in the largest diagnostic-test validation (146 patients with pituitary disease, 203 controls)

items.t: In 17 healthy men, intravenous GHRP-6 raised GH dose-dependently, peaking at 45 minutes and back to baseline by 210 minutes (Ilson 1989). It also worked when swallowed, with under 1% absorption (Hartman 1992).

GHRH plus GHRP-6 was validated as a test for adult GH deficiency in studies of 125 patients and 125 controls (Popovic 2000), 146 patients and 203 controls (Leal 2002) and 83 adults after brain injury (Castro 2007).
Hunger is the hallmark effect and is what the ghrelin receptor does; controlled food-intake studies exist for its sibling GHRP-2, none that we found for GHRP-6 itself.
Cuban work reports protection in animal models of ischemia; we found no completed human trial.

more.title: More: why a GH peak is not a GH treatment
paras: A dose produces a GH burst lasting a few hours; IGF-1, the growth and repair signal, needs sustained GH to move. No multi-month study has shown repeated GHRP-6 raising IGF-1 or changing body composition, and its close relative hexarelin failed to change IGF-1, fat or lean mass over 16 weeks.

effects.headline: Hunger, short hormone surges, and almost no long-term safety data.
effects.lede: What is known comes from single doses given in clinics; the diagnostic studies reported no side effects of note. Nobody has followed healthy adults through months of repeated use.

disc.title: Stopping because of side effects
disc.text: Not measurable: no multi-dose human trial exists. In one diagnostic study of 49 patients and 20 controls, a single dose caused no side effects (Alaioubi 2009).

unique.title: Hunger, and FDA's flagged risks
unique.text: Strong hunger soon after a dose is the signature effect. FDA places GHRP-6 on its Category 2 list of compounding substances with significant safety risks, citing an immune-reaction risk for certain routes, possible effects on cortisol and on blood sugar through reduced insulin sensitivity, and limited safety information overall.

more.title: More: what a GH-raising drug can do over time
paras: Sustained GH can cause fluid retention, joint pain, carpal-tunnel-type tingling and higher blood sugar; GH-axis trials monitor for these and exclude active cancer because GH and IGF-1 can promote tumour growth. Whether repeated GHRP-6 produces enough GH to cause them has never been studied.

more.title: More: the good side effects
paras: Reliable GH release in people with a working pituitary, which is why it made a useful diagnostic test. No benefit beyond that has been shown in humans.

urgent.title: Symptoms that need a doctor
items: Spreading redness, pus or fever at an injection site; hives, facial swelling or trouble breathing
Marked thirst, frequent urination or blurred vision; or shakiness, sweating and confusion
Tingling hands, swollen hands or feet, or new joint pain that does not settle
urgent.note: Get medical care and say exactly what product was used.

levels.nopk: One published pharmacokinetic study exists (Cabrales et al., 2013: nine healthy men, Cuba), but we could not read its half-life figure in the original paper, so no simulator is shown rather than copy a number second-hand. What is documented: GH peaks about 45 minutes after an intravenous dose and is back to baseline by about 3.5 hours.

explain.t: GHRP-6 is cleared within hours; each dose makes one GH burst and nothing accumulates between doses.
Muscle, fat and healing effects of GH depend on sustained IGF-1, which no human study has shown GHRP-6 raising.

more.title: More: why there is no chart
paras: The level charts need a verified half-life and a trial dosing schedule; GHRP-6 has no treatment regimen, and we did not verify its half-life from the primary paper.

more.title: More: what blood levels could not tell you anyway
paras: Products sold as GHRP-6 are unverified: customs seizures have contained GHRP-6 in vials sold as growth hormone, and a German laboratory found a glycine-modified GHRP-6 analogue, never tested in any human, in black-market products.

trials.headline: No trial is recruiting for GHRP-6 as a treatment; its human record is pharmacology and diagnostics.
trials.lede: GHRP-6's human studies were hormone experiments and test validations, mostly from 1989 to 2009. Nothing registered today would change its status.

more.title: More: what the diagnostic studies involved
paras: Participants received one intravenous injection of GHRH plus GHRP-6 in hospital, with blood drawn over the next hour or two to measure the GH peak, as a replacement for the risky insulin tolerance test. The studies say nothing about taking GHRP-6 repeatedly.

running.title: Trials that have been run
items: Healthy men, 1989: intravenous GHRP-6 versus saline in 17 men; dose-dependent GH rise peaking at 45 minutes (Ilson et al.); oral GHRP-6 released GH despite under 1% absorption (Hartman 1992).
Diagnostic validations, 1995–2009: GHRH plus GHRP-6 in hundreds of adults with pituitary disease and controls; judged safe and reliable (Popovic 2000; Leal 2002; Castro 2007; Alaioubi 2009).
Pharmacokinetics, 2013: single doses in nine healthy men, Cuba (Cabrales et al.).
Not run: any placebo-controlled trial for muscle, fat, healing, heart protection or ageing.

find.text: Searching the public registry for "GHRP-6" returns historical diagnostic studies, not treatment trials.

status.headline: Not approved anywhere. Not legally compoundable in the U.S. Banned in sport.

items.label: Canada
items.text: No GHRP-6 product holds a Health Canada DIN. Health Canada's April 2026 advisory treats injectable peptides as prescription drugs and says a "research use only" label does not make them legal; it reports border seizures and won a permanent injunction against a Québec online seller in July 2026.

items.label: United States
items.text: Never FDA-approved; an FDA-commissioned review (2021) found no approved product in 13 registries. FDA lists it in 503A Category 3 (nominated without adequate support; May 2026) and 503B Category 2 (significant safety risks; April 2026), so it cannot legally be compounded. FDA's August 24, 2026 warning letters to five online peptide sellers rejected "research use only" labelling.

items.label: Sport
items.text: Prohibited at all times under WADA's 2026 Prohibited List (S2, GH-releasing peptides; GHRP-6 is named); GHRP findings have appeared in doping control since 2014.

cards.title: What "research use only" really means
cards.text: Regulators judge a product by how it is sold, not its label: human-dose vials, bacteriostatic water, dosing calculators and health claims count as intended human use. Testing shows why that matters:
items: Norway's doping laboratory tested 21 seized vials sold as growth hormone: only 5 were; 3 were GHRP-6 and others CJC-1295, sermorelin or ipamorelin (Henninge 2011). A 2007 seizure of unmarked "salt" from China turned out to be GHRP-6 (Henninge 2008).

Australia's sports drug testing laboratory analysed 200+ black-market peptide products: about 25% matched the label, 25% contained no peptide, and one "growth hormone" product contained pig insulin (Sport Integrity Australia).
A German anti-doping laboratory found Gly-GHRP-6, a chemically altered GHRP-6 never tested in humans, in black-market products (Krug 2018).
cards.note: No regulator has checked any online GHRP-6 product for identity, strength, sterility or endotoxin.

cards.title: If someone has already used a product sold as GHRP-6
cards.text: See a doctor if any of these appear, and bring the vial:
items: Fever, or redness and pus at an injection site
Marked thirst, frequent urination, or shakiness and confusion
Swelling of hands, feet or face; new joint pain or tingling hands
Severe abdominal pain or persistent vomiting
cards.note: Report a reaction to MedEffect Canada (canada.ca/medeffect) or, in the U.S., FDA MedWatch (fda.gov/medwatch).

more.title: More: U.S. peptide policy is moving, but not for GHRP-6
paras: In July 2026 an FDA advisory committee recommended six other peptides for the compounding list, and on October 14–15, 2026 HHS sent a peptide "Interim Access Policy" to the White House; its terms are not public. GHRP-6 was not reviewed and stays on FDA's Category 2 list.
